questions.q: If two angles form a linear pair and one of them measures $75^\circ$, what is the measure of the other angle?
questions.a: The measure is $105^\circ$. Students who answer $25^\circ$ or $180^\circ$ likely confused the linear pair property with complementary angles ($90^\circ$) or thought the total sum must equal the single given angle, failing to recall that a straight line measures $180^\circ$.

questions.q: Explain why the sum of the angles in a linear pair is always $180^\circ$ rather than $360^\circ$.
questions.a: A linear pair rests on a straight line, which represents a straight angle measuring $180^\circ$ (half of a full circle's $360^\circ$). Students who believe it is $360^\circ$ confuse a straight line with a complete point rotation or full circle.

questions.q: Two adjacent angles on a straight line are given as $(3x)^\circ$ and $(2x + 30)^\circ$. Find the exact numerical value of $x$.
questions.a:
Steps: 
1. Recognize that the angles form a linear pair, so their sum is $180^\circ$.
2. Set up the equation: $3x + 2x + 30 = 180$.
3. Combine like terms: $5x + 30 = 180$.
4. Subtract 30 from both sides: $5x = 150$.
5. Divide by 5: $x = 30$. 
The final answer is $x = 30$. Students who subtract $30$ from $180$ before combining terms or make arithmetic errors during division will arrive at incorrect values like $36$ or $50$.

questions.q: Compare an angle of $95^\circ$ and its linear pair partner with two angles measuring $80^\circ$ and $100^\circ$. Can both sets be classified as linear pairs? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: Only the pair summing to $180^\circ$ ($95^\circ$ and $85^\circ$, assuming the first scenario) forms a valid linear pair because linear pairs require adjacent angles on a straight line summing to $180^\circ$. While $80^\circ$ and $100^\circ$ sum to $180^\circ$, they are not necessarily adjacent or sharing a common arm on a straight line unless explicitly stated. Students who say yes to both focus only on the numerical sum of $180^\circ$ and ignore the geometric requirement of adjacency on a straight line.

questions.q: Evaluate the following student's solution: "For a linear pair where angle A = $4x$ and angle B = $2x$, I wrote $4x \times 2x = 180$, so $8x^2 = 180$." Is this correct? Identify the error and provide the correct working.
questions.a: The student's solution is incorrect. The error is multiplying the angles instead of adding them ($4x + 2x = 180$). Correct working: $4x + 2x = 180 \Rightarrow 6x = 180 \Rightarrow x = 30$. Students who defend the student's solution fail to understand that linear pairs combine by addition (sum equals $180^\circ$), not multiplication.

questions.q: Construct a word problem involving a carpenter cutting a wooden plank where two resulting edge angles form a linear pair, using an algebraic expression with an unknown variable $p$, and state the sum equation.
questions.a: A carpenter cuts a straight wooden plank into two sections meeting at a joint. One section forms an angle of $(5p - 10)^\circ$ and the adjacent section forms an angle of $(3p + 30)^\circ$. The equation is $(5p - 10) + (3p + 30) = 180$. A poor answer would fail to set up an algebraic equation or use an incorrect sum like $90^\circ$ or $360^\circ$.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A linear pair of angles is a pair of adjacent angles formed when two lines ______, whose non-common arms form a straight line and whose angle measures always sum up to exactly 180 degrees.

Fill in the blank: Imagine walking along a straight ______ on an Indian highway, then turning sharply onto a side road to enter a petrol pump; the two paths you took form angles along the straight edge of the main road.

Fill in the blank: A linear pair of angles is a pair of adjacent angles formed when two lines intersect, whose non-common arms form a straight line and whose angle measures always sum up to exactly ______ degrees.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Can identify linear pairs from geometric diagrams, set up linear equations using the 180-degree sum property, and accurately solve for unknown angle variables in multi-step algebraic problems.
